papers.title: Chronic neuropeptide S treatment improves sleep architecture and reduces Aβ-related pathology in APP/PS1 mice.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances frequently occur in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Although neuropeptide S (NPS) promotes wakefulness through the widely expressed NPS receptor (NPSR), its role in AD-related sleep dysregulation is unclear. To investigate the effects of chronic NPS administration on AD-related sleep disturbances beyond its acute wake-promoting effects. NPSR expression was examined in the hypothalamus and hippocampus of APPswe/PS1dE9 (APP/PS1) mice, a double-transgenic mouse model of AD. Mice received intracerebroventricular NPS (1 nmol/day) for 14 days. Sleep-wake states were classified as wakefulness, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. Sleep architecture and amyloid-β (Aβ)-related pathology were assessed in mice. Cell-associated Aβ levels, extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) phosphorylation, and autophagy-related proteins were examined in BV2 cells. Sleep responses to subsequent intracerebroventricular Aβ₁-₄₂ administration were examined in NPS-treated APP/PS1 mice. APP/PS1 mice had lower NPSR protein levels in the hypothalamus and hippocampus than wild-type (WT) controls. Compared with saline-treated APP/PS1 mice, NPS-treated mice showed increased NREM sleep, reduced wakefulness, and lower Aβ-related pathology. Changes in sleep amounts were most evident during the light phase. Subsequent Aβ₁-₄₂ administration increased wakefulness and reduced NREM sleep mainly during the dark phase. It also shortened NREM episodes during the light phase. In BV2 cells, NPS altered cell-associated Aβ levels and increased ERK phosphorylation. NPS treatment was also associated with higher LC3B-II and lower p62 levels. SCH772984 attenuated the NPS-associated changes in autophagy-related proteins and cell-associated Aβ. Chronic NPS administration improved sleep architecture and reduced Aβ-related pathology in APP/PS1 mice. The BV2 findings suggest possible involvement of ERK signaling and autophagy-related processes in cellular Aβ handling.

papers.title: Associations between the duration of outdoor sunlight exposure and the risk of developing 134 different diseases.
papers.abstract: Existing studies of sunlight exposure and health have mainly focused on specific organs, particularly the skin and eyes, while associations with other organs and systems remain largely unexplored. We aimed to comprehensively examine the associations between outdoor sunlight exposure duration and 134 diseases. Using UK Biobank data, summer and winter outdoor durations were collected by questionnaire, and average daily exposure was calculated as their arithmetic mean. Incident diseases were defined using 525 three-character ICD-10 codes. Cox proportional hazards models estimated associations, and restricted cubic splines assessed potential nonlinearity. Among 281,282 participants [mean (SD) age, 55.81 (8.07) years; 55.79% female], 1,115,346 incident cases occurred during a median follow-up of more than 13.4 years. After false discovery rate correction, sunlight exposure was associated with 36 diseases, with hazard ratios ranging from 0.914 to 1.086. For example, each additional hour of average exposure was associated with higher risks of malignant melanoma of the skin (HR = 1.052, 95% CI 1.012-1.094), obesity (1.039, 1.027-1.052), cerebrovascular diseases (1.028, 1.011-1.046), and osteoarthritis (1.042, 1.033-1.052), and lower risks of osteoporosis (0.975, 0.957-0.994), disorders of mineral metabolism (0.968, 0.944-0.992), and pressure ulcers (0.947, 0.916-0.979). Thirty diseases, including depression, anxiety, sleep disorders, arrhythmias, iron deficiency anemia, and kidney failure, showed U-shaped associations. Outdoor sunlight exposure duration showed positive, inverse, and nonlinear associations with a broad range of diseases. These findings highlight the potential importance of moderate exposure and appropriate sun protection but require validation in other populations.

papers.title: Case Report: When obstructive sleep apnea is not benign-nasopharyngeal rhabdomyosarcoma in a 3-year-old.
papers.abstract: Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is common in children and is most frequently associated with adenotonsillar hypertrophy. However, similar symptoms may occasionally reflect more serious upper airway pathology. We report a previously healthy 3-year-old boy who presented with snoring, mouth breathing, witnessed apneas, and persistent nasal obstruction in the setting of an acute viral upper respiratory illness. Initial flexible nasopharyngeal endoscopy was limited by copious secretions and poor cooperation, with no obvious mass identified. The subsequent development of epistaxis prompted repeat endoscopic evaluation, which revealed a left-sided nasopharyngeal mass. Imaging demonstrated an aggressive parameningeal lesion with skull base erosion and extension into the cavernous sinus. Histopathological examination, supported by positive immunohistochemical staining for desmin, myogenin, and MyoD1, confirmed embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma. The patient received VAC-based chemotherapy and proton radiotherapy, with subsequent tumor regression and stable findings on long-term imaging follow-up; he remained clinically well approximately four years after completion of therapy. This case highlights the potential for diagnostic anchoring when common symptoms of pediatric OSA coexist with apparently benign conditions such as adenotonsillar hypertrophy or an acute respiratory infection. Incomplete nasopharyngeal visualization should not be considered reassuring when symptoms persist or evolve. The emergence of red-flag features, particularly epistaxis, progressive nasal obstruction, or failure to improve as expected, should prompt timely reassessment and consideration of cross-sectional imaging to exclude an underlying structural lesion.

papers.title: Pan-genomic dissection of the CCT gene family in wheat reveals evolutionary dynamics and regulatory divergence.
papers.abstract: The CCT (CONSTANS, CO-LIKE, and TIMING OF CAB EXPRESSION 1) gene family regulates flowering time, circadian rhythm maintenance, and abiotic stress responses. However, previous investigations in wheat have relied on single-reference genomes, limiting the understanding of inter-varietal structural variation. Here, we performed a pan-genomic analysis of the CCT gene family across 16 wheat accessions. Copy numbers varied from 27 in diploid Triticum urartu to 69-103 in modern common wheat cultivars, with subgenomic contributions displaying an A > D > B gradient. Orthogroup classification based on the 12 T. aestivum cultivars identified 22 Core, 9 Softcore, 2 Dispensable, and 2 predicted Private orthogroups, all under strong purifying selection; the Private orthogroups require assembly-level validation because most cultivars used projected gene models. Protein-protein interaction network analysis identified a small set of highly connected nodes, with enrichment in circadian rhythm and photoperiodic flowering pathways, though this is largely expected given the query sequences; DeepGOPlus annotation further supported their roles as transcriptional regulators. Hexaploid wheat possessed longer mRNA lengths than tetraploids and diploids, but this may partly reflect annotation gaps. Promoter cis-elements were conserved across subgenomes, while paired analysis of homoeologous triads revealed significant expression divergence among subgenome copies. Tissue-specific profiling in Chinese Spring identified grain-preferential genes enriched for seed-specific elements, and stress treatments revealed candidate cis-elements, with WUN-motif and CGTCA-motif remaining significant after FDR correction. These findings provide a comprehensive view of CCT gene family evolution and regulatory diversification, offering candidate genes for stress tolerance and yield improvement in wheat.

papers.title: Restorative free time and psychological distress among employed family caregivers of individuals with cognitive impairment: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Employed family caregivers of individuals with cognitive impairment often need to balance work responsibilities, caregiving tasks, and their own daily lives. Although caregiving burden is commonly discussed in terms of time spent caregiving, less attention has been paid to whether caregivers have enough time to recover from these demands. This study examined the associations of daily time-use factors, including restorative free time, sleep duration, working hours, and caregiving duration, with psychological distress among employed family caregivers of individuals with cognitive impairment. A cross-sectional study was conducted as part of the Sustaining for Aging Dementia Relatives Support and Employment project in Japan. Questionnaires were distributed to family caregivers, and data from 210 employed caregivers were analyzed. Psychological distress was assessed using the Kessler 6 scale. Modified Poisson regression with robust variance estimation was used to estimate prevalence ratios (PRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for the associations between daily time use and psychological distress. In supplementary analyses, logistic regression was used to explore factors associated with severely limited restorative free time (<1 h/day), including care recipient characteristics such as functional status and long-term care certification. Caregivers with less than 1 h of restorative free time per day had a significantly higher prevalence of psychological distress than those with 3 h or more. Short sleep duration (<6 h/day) was also associated with a higher prevalence of psychological distress, whereas working hours and caregiving duration were not significantly associated with psychological distress after multivariable adjustment. Severely limited restorative free time and short sleep duration were associated with a higher prevalence of psychological distress among employed family caregivers. Limited restorative free time may therefore serve as a potential marker of psychological distress in this population. However, the cross-sectional design does not establish the temporal or causal direction of these associations.

papers.title: Serotonergic control of valence processing in amygdalo- striaterminalis circuits.
papers.abstract: Valence, a hedonic value assigned to sensory stimuli that determines subsequent behaviors, is a fundamental organizing principle of affective states and emotional behaviors. Valence influences physiological processes across multiple organ systems - effects that may be mediated in part by the serotonergic (5-HT) system, which itself has widespread distribution throughout the body. The brain serotonergic system projects to the amygdala and its extended structure, the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BNST), regions heavily implicated in valence encoding. Despite their anatomical and functional connectivity, the amygdala and BNST express distinct 5-HT receptor subtypes, receive heterogeneous 5-HT projections, and process valence differently. The current study examines the significance of 5-HT projections in the computation of valence in the CeA and BNST. Here, multi-site in vivo electrophysiology was combined with anterograde chemogenetic modulation of 5-HT terminals in either the BNST or the CeA, while recording from both regions during valence presentation tasks where mice were exposed to the odorants of saline (neutral), opposite-sex urine (positive), and trimethylthiazoline (TMT, negative valence) in a counterbalanced manner. Neural responses were then compared across the neutral, appetitive, and aversive stimuli. Our results showed dorsal raphe 5-HT activation in the BNST supported valence coding in the CeA and BNST during stimulus presentation. During the post-stimulus phase, this modulation engaged only CeA-supported valence coding. Conversely, the inhibition of 5-HT terminals in the BNST supported local valence coding. Dorsal raphe 5-HT activation in the CeA enhanced valence coding in both the CeA and BNST only after stimulus offset. However, its suppression in the CeA enhanced valence coding in both the CeA and BNST during and after stimulus presentation. Taken together, our results showed that dorsal raphe serotonergic modulation creates a phasic response pattern in the CeA/BNST circuit by moderating response timing relative to stimulus valence.

papers.title: Metabolomic signatures associated with muscle dysfunction during the SIRIUS-21 space analog mission.
papers.abstract: There is growing interest in exploring outer space to expand scientific knowledge and access valuable material resources. However, progress is limited by the harsh space environment, including microgravity, ionizing radiation, isolation and confinement (IC), disrupted circadian rhythms, and nutritional challenges. These stressors contribute to health problems across multiple organ systems, particularly the musculoskeletal, immune, renal/urinary, and cardiovascular systems. Although we have extensive insight into skeletal muscle pathophysiological changes induced by these spaceflight-related stressors, the molecular mechanisms underlying functional alterations caused by prolonged IC in skeletal muscle remain incompletely understood. During the 8-month SIRIUS-21 space analog mission, five participants (3 males, 2 females) underwent plasma and saliva sampling and electromyography (EMG) assessment at five time points: baseline (Ingress), early, mid, and late isolation and confinement (IC), and 14 days post-mission (Egress). Metabolites were analyzed by LC-MS/MS. Longitudinal metabolite changes were assessed using repeated-measures ANOVA with Tukey HSD post hoc testing, and direct metabolite-EMG relationships were explored using Spearman rank correlations. Metabolomic profiling identified 45 skeletal muscle-related metabolites with nominally significant longitudinal changes (p < 0.0001-0.05): 8 were detected in both plasma and saliva, 26 only in plasma, and 11 only in saliva. Direct exploratory Spearman correlations with EMG metrics were identified for a subset of metabolites, including pipecolic acid, phenylacetic acid, L-phenylalanine, L-acetylcarnitine, L-glutamine, and pyruvaldehyde. EMG findings showed a progressive decline in muscle activation and fatigue resistance during prolonged IC, with partial recovery after egress. Exploratory sex-related analyses were interpreted descriptively because the cohort included only two females and three males. Prolonged IC was accompanied by coordinated changes in muscle function and circulating or salivary metabolites. The identified metabolites represent candidate metabolic signatures associated with muscle dysfunction and require validation in larger independent cohorts before diagnostic or therapeutic utility can be established.

papers.title: ECG Holter-based screening for sleep-disordered breathing in post-stroke patients: a large monocentric cohort study.
papers.abstract: Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB) is highly prevalent after stroke and is associated with poor functional outcomes and increased mortality, yet systematic screening remains challenging because of limited polysomnography accessibility. We evaluated three electrocardiogram (ECG)-based indices for SDB screening in a large consecutive post-stroke cohort. This retrospective single-centre cohort study included 1,929 consecutive patients hospitalised for stroke or transient ischaemic attack at Saint-Étienne University Hospital (2010-2021) who were in sinus rhythm with ECG signal quality adequate for ECG-derived respiration (EDR) analysis; patients with atrial fibrillation, pacemaker rhythm, or severe ectopy (>10% of beats) were excluded a priori. EDR, the Thoracic Impedance Disturbance Index (TIDI) and the Very Low Frequency Increment (VLFI) were compared with the simultaneous oxygen desaturation index (ODI) as reference standard. Sensitivity, specificity, accuracy and predictive values were calculated at ODI thresholds of 15/h and 30/h; a combined TIDI+EDR concordant rule was assessed as a post-hoc exploratory analysis. The cohort comprised 61% males (mean age 65.9 years). Suspected SDB (ODI ≥ 5/h) was present in 74.6% of patients, moderate-to-severe SDB (ODI ≥ 15/h) in 38.9% and severe SDB (ODI ≥ 30/h) in 17.1%. For ODI ≥ 15/h (n = 750), TIDI had the highest sensitivity (93.3%) and negative predictive value (90.8%), whereas EDR had higher specificity (80.2%) and accuracy (74.2%); the combined rule reached 85.2% specificity and 72.9% positive predictive value. For ODI ≥ 30/h (n = 330), EDR showed specificity of 92.4% and accuracy of 85.2%, and the combined rule 95.4% and 86.9%, respectively. VLFI performed poorly across all metrics. ECG-based tools can identify post-stroke patients at high risk of SDB using routine cardiac monitoring. The complementary profiles of TIDI (rule-out) and EDR (rule-in) support a sequential screening approach, which requires prospective validation against polysomnography. VLFI is unsuitable for elderly stroke populations because of age-related autonomic dysfunction. Because patients with atrial fibrillation, pacemaker rhythm or severe arrhythmia were excluded, the findings may not generalise to this higher-arrhythmia-burden subgroup, who may also be at higher risk of SDB.

papers.title: Circadian rhythm and cancer-related pain: a systematic review of preclinical and clinical evidence.
papers.abstract: Cancer-related pain and neuropathy are common complications that substantially affect quality of life. Circadian rhythms regulate biological processes involved in pain and treatment response; however, evidence linking circadian biology and treatment timing with cancer-related pain and neuropathy remains limited and heterogeneous, and the underlying mechanisms are incompletely understood. This systematic review aimed to evaluate these relationships and their potential biological mechanisms and clinical implications across clinical and preclinical studies. PRISMA-guided systematic review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251174524). PubMed and Web of Science were searched for original human and preclinical studies published up to October 20, 2025. Eligible studies evaluated circadian rhythms, clock genes, or circadian-based treatment timing in relation to cancer- or treatment-related pain, neuropathy, or analgesic response. Direct pain-related and indirect neuropathy outcomes were synthesized separately. Risk of bias was assessed using JBI tools for human studies and SYRCLE for preclinical studies. Thirty-nine studies were included: 35 human (89.7%) and 4 preclinical studies (10.3%). Most populations included mixed cancer types (10/39, 25.6%). Cohort or observational studies represented 38.5% and clinical trials represented 28.2%, with 16/39 (41%) studies published between 2015 and 2025. Clinical findings were heterogeneous, with temporal variation reported for cancer-related pain and analgesic requirements, while chronotherapy studies suggested potential reductions in treatment-related neuropathy and neurotoxicity, representing indirect pain-related evidence. Potential mechanisms were reported or discussed in 15/35 (42.9%) human studies and were largely hypothesis-generating, involving HPA-axis/cortisol dysregulation, drug pharmacokinetics, and metabolism, inflammatory signaling, and circadian-regulatory pathways; direct clinical clock-gene evidence was limited to RORA. Four preclinical studies provided experimental evidence implicating clock genes (PER2, BMAL1, and REV-ERBα/β), oxidative stress, neuronal injury, drug metabolism, and neuroinflammatory (IL-6/LCN2) pathways. Methodological quality was limited, with high risk of bias in 10/15 (67%) cohort studies and 8/11 (73%) clinical trials and high or unclear risk across several preclinical domains. Current evidence suggests a potential relationship between circadian biology and cancer- and treatment-related pain, analgesic response, and neuropathy. Clinical findings remain heterogeneous, human mechanistic evidence is predominantly hypothesis-generating, and experimental evidence remains limited. Prospective mechanistic studies are needed to support future circadian-informed approaches for cancer pain management. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251174524, identifier CRD420251174524.

papers.title: Multimodal EEG-fNIRS complexity analysis can reveal the neurovascular coupling change with aging.
papers.abstract: This study aimed to investigate age-related changes in neurovascular coupling (NVC) function of the brain using a multimodal electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) approach combined with nonlinear entropy analysis. The study included 20 young adults and 20 older adults. We simultaneously recorded EEG and fNIRS data during four cognitive tasks (auditory attention task, verbal fluency task, upper limb motor task, and recognition memory task). We calculated sample entropy (SampEn) and conditional entropy (CondEn) for five EEG frequency sub-bands (Delta: 1-4 Hz, Theta: 4-8 Hz, Alpha: 8-12 Hz, Beta: 12-30 Hz, Gamma: 30-40 Hz) as well as for fNIRS signals (oxygenated hemoglobin and deoxygenated hemoglobin, HbO and HbR) to quantify neural and hemodynamic complexity of brain activity. Additionally, cross-sample entropy (Cross-SampEn) and cross-conditional entropy (Cross-CondEn) between EEG and fNIRS signals were computed to evaluate NVC function. Group differences were assessed using analysis of covariance (ANCOVA), with age group as the fixed factor and sex and years of education as covariates. Older adults showed higher EEG SampEn or CondEn in selected frequency bands during the auditory attention task and the encoding and recognition phases of the recognition memory task. For fNIRS, older adults showed lower HbO SampEn during memory recognition. Cross-modal analysis showed lower beta-HbR Cross-SampEn during the left upper limb motor task and higher theta-HbR Cross-SampEn during memory encoding in older adults. Aging is associated with task-specific alterations in neural complexity, hemodynamic complexity, and the cross-modal temporal relationship between EEG and fNIRS signals. These findings suggest that age-related changes in NVC-related dynamics are better characterized as dynamic reorganization rather than a uniform enhancement or impairment, and support the potential of multimodal entropy analysis for characterizing age-related neurovascular coupling change.

papers.title: Pain, Sleep, and Affective Symptoms in Primary Dysmenorrhea: A Symptom Network and Insular Connectivity Study.
papers.abstract: Primary dysmenorrhea (PDM) is a prevalent gynecological pain condition frequently accompanied by sleep disturbance and affective symptoms. Although neuroimaging studies have reported altered brain function in PDM, how menstrual pain relates to its multidimensional symptom profile remains incompletely understood. A total of 113 women with PDM and 105 healthy controls (HCs) underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging during menstruation. Clinical symptoms, including the Visual Analog Scale (VAS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS), Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS), and Self-Rating Depression Scale (SDS), were assessed using standardized questionnaires. Symptom network analysis was performed to identify core clinical symptoms in PDM. Subsequently, seed-based resting-state functional connectivity (rs-FC) analyses of insular subregions were conducted. Associations between altered insular connectivity and core clinical symptoms were further examined in patients with PDM. Symptom network analysis identified sleep disturbance and affective symptom dimensions as central or bridging features within the clinical symptom network of PDM. Compared with HCs, patients with PDM exhibited increased rs-FC between the ventral anterior insula (vAI) and regions involved in salience and cognitive-emotional processing. Exploratory Spearman correlation analyses revealed nominal positive associations between right vAI-anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) connectivity and sleep disturbance (ρ = 0.21, uncorrected P = 0.026) and anxiety (ρ = 0.26, uncorrected P = 0.005). However, neither association survived FDR correction for multiple comparisons (adjusted P = 0.194 and 0.075, respectively). These findings suggest that altered anterior insula functional connectivity may represent a neural correlate of sleep disturbance and affective symptoms in PDM. Integrating symptom network analysis with insula-centered functional connectivity analysis offers complementary perspectives on menstrual pain and its co-occurring symptoms.

papers.title: Potential Applications of Brain-Computer Interface Technology in the Rehabilitation of Patients with Anxiety Disorders: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Anxiety disorders are among the most prevalent mental disorders worldwide and can cause persistent impairment in emotional regulation, cognition, and social functioning. Pharmacotherapy, psychotherapy, exercise, and non-invasive brain stimulation are widely used, yet their effectiveness may be constrained by dependence liability, interindividual variability, treatment engagement, incomplete response, and limited objective measures of treatment processes. Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) acquire, decode, and feed back neural signals-most commonly electroencephalography (EEG), functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), or real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging (rt-fMRI)-thereby converting anxiety-related brain activity into targets that can be monitored, trained, or used to trigger intervention. This narrative review examines the mechanistic rationale for BCI-assisted anxiety rehabilitation, technological approaches across levels of invasiveness, and integration with pharmacological, psychological, and exercise-based care. Current evidence indicates that EEG has been used for both anxiety-state recognition and neurofeedback; rt-fMRI enables targeted modulation of deep emotion-related networks and functional connectivity; and fNIRS offers promise for portable prefrontal monitoring and as an input signal for closed-loop systems. Invasive closed-loop systems can directly record from and stimulate local or deep circuits, but anxiety-related evidence is derived mainly from animal studies, patients undergoing intracranial monitoring, and neurological populations with comorbid anxiety, and therefore demonstrates technical feasibility rather than efficacy in primary anxiety disorders. Overall, BCIs are better positioned as potential adjuncts to established care than as replacements. The field remains limited by small, single-center studies, inadequate follow-up, heterogeneous acquisition and training protocols, and unresolved governance of neural data. Because this is a narrative review without a formal risk-of-bias assessment or meta-analysis, its conclusions should be regarded as exploratory. Multicenter randomized controlled trials, harmonized technical and reporting standards, cross-device external validation, and risk-proportionate ethical and regulatory frameworks are needed to determine whether BCIs can be translated from proof of concept into safe, effective, and implementable tools for anxiety rehabilitation.

papers.title: Differences in pulse oximetry saturation from sea level to high altitude among subjects with and without respiratory disease. A population-based, cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Oxygen saturation (SpO2) is used to detect hypoxemia and guide oxygen therapy, but its interpretation varies with altitude, age, and lung disease. Although >500 million people live at ≥1,500 m, population-based data comparing SpO2 across altitudes in adults with and without chronic respiratory disease are scarce. We aimed to compare SpO2 between these groups from sea level to 3,030 m, identify factors associated with SpO2, and describe SpO2 by altitude and age in adults without respiratory disease. We hypothesized that SpO2 would be lower in participants with respiratory disease, with differences increasing with altitude. PREPOCOL II is a population-based, cross-sectional study with a probabilistic, two-stage, clustered sampling design to estimate the prevalence and risk factors for respiratory disease among adults ≥40 years in Colombian cities at different altitudes (18-3030 m). All participants completed a standardized questionnaire, spirometry, and SpO2 measurement. Participants with respiratory disease (RDP), including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, asthma, chronic bronchitis, obstructive sleep apnea, and interstitial lung disease, were compared with controls using Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis tests, multivariable linear regression, and comparisons of altitude coefficients between groups. A total of 1146 RDP and 4613 controls were included. RDP were older, and had lower BMI and lung function. SpO2 was lower in RDP than in controls at all altitudes and decreased in both groups as altitude and age increased (p<0.001). In multivariable models, altitude showed the strongest association with SpO2 (standardized β -0.69 in controls and -0.71 in RDP), followed by age and BMI (and FEV1 in RDP). The decrease in SpO2 per unit of altitude was larger in RDP (B -1.15 vs. -0.80; difference p<0.001), and the between-group difference became evident at ~1,500 m (median 97.0% vs. 95.5%). Among lifelong residents living at altitudes from sea level to 3,030 m, SpO2 was lower in RDP than in controls. SpO2 decreased with altitude and age in both groups, with altitude being the variable most strongly associated with SpO2. SpO2 values should be interpreted in relation to specific altitude and age. In RDP, the lower SpO2 was most evident at altitudes of ~1,500 m and above.

papers.title: Habitual sleep duration and spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage: a prospective UK Biobank cohort study with supporting hospital-based neurosurgical data.
papers.abstract: Abnormal sleep duration has been associated with stroke, but evidence specific to spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage (sICH) remains limited. We conducted a two-part observational study. The prospective UK Biobank analysis included 314,236 participants free of sICH at baseline, among whom 1,387 developed incident sICH. The supporting cross-sectional hospital analysis included 312 patients with imaging-confirmed sICH and 515 non-ICH neurosurgical controls from Jinjiang Municipal Hospital. Habitual sleep duration was categorized as short (<7 h/day), normal (7-9 h/day), or long (>9 h/day). Cox proportional hazards models [hazard ratios (HRs)] and logistic regression [odds ratios (ORs)] were used, together with restricted cubic splines, additional adjustment for medications, blood pressure, and indicators of prevalent ill health, and multiple imputation of missing data. A systemic inflammatory marker score and interaction analyses with false-discovery-rate correction were examined as secondary, exploratory analyses. Compared with normal sleep, short and long sleep were associated with higher incident sICH risk in the UK Biobank [adjusted HRs 1.14 (95% CI 1.03-1.26) and 1.55 (1.15-2.09)]; the short-sleep association was modest and less robust in sensitivity analyses. Corresponding cross-sectional ORs in the hospital dataset were 1.49 (1.04-2.13) and 2.05 (1.17-3.59), respectively. Restricted cubic splines suggested U-shaped associations in both datasets, with the lowest estimated hazard or odds at approximately 7-8 h/day. Estimates were similar after additional confounder adjustment (HRs 1.10 and 1.43 for short and long sleep, respectively) and multiple imputation (HRs 1.13 and 1.50, respectively). No interaction, including with inflammatory marker burden, remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction, and adjustment for the marker score changed the estimates only modestly. Both short and long sleep duration were associated with higher incident sICH risk in the UK Biobank and higher odds of sICH in the hospital dataset, with stronger and more consistent associations observed for long sleep. Systemic inflammatory markers neither explained nor reliably modified these associations, and because long sleep may partly reflect prevalent ill health, the long-sleep association warrants cautious interpretation. Sleep duration may be a useful marker of sICH susceptibility.

papers.title: Visualization of super-selective Wada with computed tomography perfusion: toward a novel option in preoperative functional mapping.
papers.abstract: The Wada test has long been a well-established method for evaluating hemispheric dominance and functional localization; however, it has not been established as a visualizable functional imaging modality. Recently, the super-selective Wada test (ssWada) has emerged as a technique enabling more localized functional evaluation. By selectively catheterizing distal cerebral arterial branches, ssWada enables territory-based functional evaluation with higher spatial resolution than conventional approaches. In this study, we combined ssWada with computed tomography perfusion (CTP) to visualize pharmacologically inactivated brain regions preoperatively. These data were further fused with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and CT to propose a novel functional mapping approach delineating the relationship between perfusion-defined functional territories, lesions, and seizure onset zone (SOZ)-related stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG) contacts. Patients who underwent ssWada for preoperative evaluation of brain tumors or drug-resistant epilepsy at our institution were included. During ssWada, propofol was selectively injected via a microcatheter into the ICA and distal branches of the middle cerebral artery (MCA), as well as the anterior or posterior cerebral artery when necessary. Perfusion territories were simultaneously visualized using CTP. These datasets were subsequently fused with MRI and post-SEEG CT to evaluate the spatial relationship between perfusion-defined functional territories, lesions, and SOZ-related SEEG contacts. Among the 23 patients, hemispheric dominance was left in 18 patients (78.3%), bilateral in 3 (13.0%), and right in 2 (8.7%). No complications were observed. In the MCA superior trunk territory, repetition, naming, and reading tasks showed positive rates of approximately 70%. In contrast, in the inferior trunk territory, repetition and reading demonstrated high positive rates (93.8%), whereas naming positivity was lower (56.3%). Fusion with MRI and post-SEEG CT enabled spatial visualization of lesions and SOZ-related SEEG contacts within perfusion-defined functional territories, facilitating individualized functional-anatomical assessment for surgical planning. ssWada combined with CTP enables territory-based visualization of pharmacologically inactivated brain regions and provides a novel preoperative functional mapping approach with high spatial resolution. Fusion with MRI and post-SEEG CT further facilitates individualized functional-anatomical assessment of lesions and SOZ-related networks. These findings support the clinical utility of ssWada-CTP fusion imaging as a novel strategy for individualized preoperative functional brain mapping.

papers.title: Fatigue after transient ischemic attack: cross-sectional associations with comorbidities, activities of daily living and social participation.
papers.abstract: Fatigue is a common symptom during the first year after transient ischemic attack (TIA), but its long-term persistence remain unclear. This study aim to assessed long-term perceived fatigue after TIA and to evaluated associated comorbidities and functional consequences. This observational and cross-sectional study included 431 community-dwelling adults assessed 1-13 years after TIA in an outpatient setting, with a 25% response rate. Fatigue was measured using the Fatigue Assessment Scale in three subgroups: first-ever TIA (n = 299), recurrent TIA (n = 54), and TIA with stroke (n = 78). Depression and anxiety were evaluated using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale, and. An activities of daily living and social participation using were determined using the Stroke Impact Scale. Multivariable ordinal linear regression analyses were performed in the first-ever TIA group to examine associations between fatigue, comorbidities and functional outcomes. In the first-ever TIA group, fatigue levels were similar across time-since-TIA strata up to 13 years (mean 21.8, standard deviation [SD] 5.2); 35% exceeded the fatigue cut-off. Fatigue in the first-ever TIA group was lower than in the recurrent TIA group (mean 23.9, SD 5.7; p < 0.05) and TIA with stroke group (mean 23.8, SD 6.5; p < 0.05). Amon participants with first-ever TIA, depression (β = 6.8, 95% confidence interval [CI] 3.5-10.1; p < 0.001), severe sleep problem (category 4: β = 3.9, 95% CI 0.9-6.8; p = 0.010) and (category 5: β = 5.9, 95% CI 2.2-9.6; p = 0.002), atrial fibrillation (β = 2.1, 95% CI 0.3-3.9; p = 0.02) and heart disease (β = 1.8, 95% CI 0.2-3.4; p = 0.03) were associated with higher fatigue. Higher fatigue was also associated with reduced activities of daily living (β = 0.15, 95% CI 0.07-0.22, p < 0.001) and lower social participation (β = 0.06, 95% CI 0.02-0.10; p = 0.004). Fatigue affected more than one-third of first-ever TIA survivors and did not differ materially across cross-sectional time-since-TIA strata up to 13 years. Greater fatigue was associated with depressive symptoms, severe sleep problems, atrial fibrillation, heart disease, and reduced daily activity and social participation. Early identification and management of fatigue and related comorbidities may improve functioning. Longitudinal studies are needed to determine temporal relationships and whether targeted management improves outcomes.

papers.title: The Cost of Control in Cardiometabolic Prevention: Insights from Sleep and Circadian Disruption.
Effects of Pore Mutations on 1/f Flicker Noise Reveal Differences in CFTR Substates.
papers.abstract: Many disease-causing mutations in the Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (CFTR), a key chloride channel, lead to cystic fibrosis by disrupting the regulation and stability of its different open and closed substates. These transitions generate rapid current fluctuations observed in patch-clamp measurements, known as flicker noise, which can reveal information about chloride flow and state dynamics in the wild type and different mutants. Using time-frequency analysis with spectrograms applied to single-channel recordings, we found that the power of higher-frequency components (10-1000 Hz) was greater during the open state than during the closed state. Frequency analysis showed 1fα noise in the fully open state (α = 0.5) and a flat power spectral density (PSD) in the closed state (α = 0). Using several pore mutants as representations of the three open states (S1, S2, and F), we found that the S2 frequency signature was similar to the fully open state (α = 0.5), whereas S1 behaved more similarly to the closed state (α = 0) in terms of flicker noise. A mutant affecting the nucleotide-binding domain (NBD) did not show changes in α. These frequency signatures were not altered by changes in electrochemical forces in the WT and may be linked to conformational changes and differences in the energy landscape and trapping of Chloride ions in energy wells during the permeation process. Using the Hurst exponent, derived from spectral analysis, we showed that S1 exhibited memoryless dynamics (H ≈ 0.5), while S2 and F showed persistent behavior (H > 0.5), indicating that memory structure depends on the substate. These experimental findings were reproduced using a transistor-based model that incorporates flicker noise and maps electrophysiological variables (τo, τc, Po, α) to circuit parameters. This allows linking functional CFTR states (C0, C1, C2, S1, S2, F) to electronic components, enabling fast, variant-specific simulations.

papers.title: A Breathable Nanomesh-Textile Electrode Interface for Integrated Multimodal Monitoring.
papers.abstract: Long-term wearable electrophysiology requires electrodes that are skin-conformal, breathable, mechanically stable, and reliably connected to electronics. Existing dry electrodes address parts of this challenge, but the interface between soft electrodes and wearable electronics remains a major source of motion artifacts, open-circuit failure, and poor long-term usability. Here, we introduce a duo-electrode interface that separates the functions of skin contact and electronic interconnection. An electrospun nanomesh serves as a tattoo electrode that conforms intimately to the skin, while a compressible conductive taffeta-foam fabric electrode embedded in a garment provides stable electrical coupling to textile-routed electronics. This architecture preserves the advantages of skin-conformal electrodes while avoiding fragile connections to electronics. We integrate the interface into a bodysuit and eyemask platform for multimodal monitoring of ECG, EMG, EOG, and body position using a centralized electronics module. The system maintains reliable signal acquisition under body motion and muscle activation, with performance comparable to or better than that of commercial hydrogel electrodes. By bridging breathable electrodes with textile-based routing, the proposed duo-electrode strategy establishes a practical method for scalable, comfortable, and long-duration wearable bioelectronic monitoring. This approach may be broadly useful for remote healthcare, rehabilitation, sleep studies, human-machine interfaces, and personalized physiological sensing.

papers.title: The Cultural and Psychosocial Significance of Latin Dancing Among Hispanic Cancer Survivors: A Qualitative Study to Inform Intervention Development.
papers.abstract: IntroductionHispanic cancer survivors experience physical and psychosocial symptom burden and face barriers to participating in physical activity (PA) programs (e.g., fatigue, lack of access, language barriers). Latin dance may be a culturally meaningful approach to promoting PA and psychosocial well-being in this population.AimsThis qualitative study explored the cultural and psychosocial significance of Latin dance among Hispanic cancer survivors to inform intervention development.MethodsFour virtual focus groups, conducted in English or Spanish, were guided by the Cultural Appropriateness Framework to discuss perceptions of Latin dance, intervention preferences, and culturally relevant program features. Transcripts were analyzed using thematic analysis.ResultsTwenty-six Hispanic cancer survivors participated. Participants had a mean age of 48.8 years (SD=14.1), 46.1% were women, and 46.2% primarily spoke Spanish. Most were from South America (46.2%), and the most common cancers were genitourinary (23.1%), gynecologic (23.1%), and gastroenterological cancers (23.1%). Three major themes emerged. First, participants described Latin dance and music as sources of cultural connection, emotional coping, and healing throughout the cancer experience. Second, participants preferred flexible and accessible intervention formats that accommodated work schedules, transportation barriers, and survivorship-related needs. Third, participants emphasized the importance of culturally meaningful program content, including familiar Latin dance styles, supportive instructors, celebratory activities, and culturally resonant music.ConclusionsLatin dance represents culturally meaningful and emotionally supportive strategies to promote PA and psychosocial well-being among Hispanic survivors. Findings support the development of culturally appropriate Latin dance interventions for Hispanic cancer survivors.

papers.title: A qualitative study of understanding the stress landscape of Bangladeshi national football players.
papers.abstract: Athletes experience multiple sources of stress that can affect their well-being and performance. However, limited research has explored these stressors among football players in Bangladesh. This study aimed to explore the types and impacts of stress experienced by Bangladeshi national footballers. A qualitative study was conducted with eight national team football players (5 male, 3 female) aged 18-25, and two national team coaches (1 male, 1 female) were purposively sampled. Semi-structured interviews were conducted via Zoom, recorded with consent, and transcribed. Transcripts were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis. Three main themes of stressors emerged: social, organizational, and personal. Social stressors included gender norms, media-related pressure, and family and community expectations. Organizational stressors included training overload, injury, institutional constraints, restricted training environments, selection uncertainty, match-related pressure, and nutrition and accommodation issues. Personal stressors included family responsibilities, financial pressure, career uncertainty, and health- and fitness-related concerns. These stressors negatively affected players' mental well-being, contributing to anxiety, emotional distress, reduced confidence, sleep disturbance, and poorer performance. Bangladeshi football players face a range of stressors at organizational, social, and personal levels. These findings highlight the importance of developing appropriate support systems, including psychological and stress-management interventions, to promote athlete well-being and performance.

papers.title: Remote STrOke Rehabilitation (ReSTORe): study protocol for a randomised controlled trial.
papers.abstract: At least one third of long-term stroke survivors living at home experience ongoing (≥6 months) mild to moderate disability including fatigue, low functional capacity, muscle weakness, anxiety, and depression. Health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and societal participation are affected, particularly after routine contact with health professionals ends. Outpatient centre-based exercise rehabilitation programmes can improve physical and mental health, but these services are rarely provided in the UK. As an alternative, online group physical and mental health rehabilitation is feasible and acceptable to people with long-term conditions and may support recovery for people with stroke. This trial aims to assess the clinical and cost-effectiveness of a supervised, live online, group exercise-based rehabilitation programme (ReSTORe) to support long-term physical and mental health recovery versus best-practice usual care, for people with mild to moderate disability, 6-36 months post-hospital discharge after stroke. ReSTORe is a pragmatic, decentralised, two-arm RCT with internal pilot and embedded economic evaluation and qualitative study. Six hundred adults with long-term mild to moderate physical and/or mental health disability after stroke (exclusions: exercise contra-indicated, severe physical disability, mental health/cognitive impairment, not living at 'home') will be randomised (1:08:1) to the ReSTORe intervention or control. The ReSTORe intervention consists of (1) 1:1 individual assessment online; (2) 10-week, once-weekly, remote group exercise programme supervised live online; (3) six online group psychosocial and motivational support sessions. The control intervention is best-practice usual care with a single 30-min 1:1 practitioner appointment and general advice on physical activity. The primary outcome is HRQoL with the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) 29+2 Profile v2.1 Preference score (PROPr) at 6 months post-randomisation. Secondary outcomes include PROMIS sub-scores: depression, fatigue, sleep, pain, physical function, social role; health utility; recurrent stroke; and health and social care use. A purposive sample of participants (n ~ 30-50) and practitioners (n ~ 8) will be interviewed to explore experiences of the trial, outcomes, and interventions. ReSTORe is the largest trial to date testing online exercise-based rehabilitation after stroke. The decentralised trial design will support inclusivity and diversity by helping to ensure productive engagement with underrepresented populations. ISRCTN ( ISRCTN81848233 ). Registered on 23 January 2025.

papers.title: A randomized controlled trial investigating the effect of thermal steam spray on nasal condition, neurological function, and sleep quality in young adults with nasal congestion and irregular sleep patterns.
papers.abstract: Intranasal thermal steam spray (ITSS) has been suggested to relieve nasal stuffiness and improve sleep-related symptoms. However, its mechanistic effects on respiratory capacity, neurological functions, including autonomic nervous system (ANS) and brain activities, remain underexplored. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the effects of an ITSS intervention on nasal condition, respiratory and neurological functions, and sleep quality in young adults with nasal congestion and irregular sleep patterns. Sixty university students (aged 20-26 years) with an average duration of nasal congestion and sleep irregularity of over three years participated. Two dormitories were randomly assigned to either a control group (CON; n = 30) or an intervention group (ITSS; n = 30). The ITSS device, delivering 43 °C thermal wet steam using jet stream (80 mm H₂O) technology, was administered for 15 min, 3 times per week, 30 min before bedtime for 8 weeks. After the intervention, subjective nasal congestion and sleep conditions deteriorated in the CON but improved in the ITSS (p < 0.001). Pulmonary outcomes, including reduced respiratory rate (p < 0.001) and increased FEV₁ (p < 0.001) and PEF (p < 0.001), improved only in the ITSS. Heart rate variability and blood pressure indices also showed favourable changes. Electroencephalographic analysis revealed increased wide band, alpha, and gamma powers in the ITSS, contrasting with declines in the CON (p < 0.05). In the ITSS group, PSQI-K components improved, with daytime dysfunction reduced by 32.78 ± 41.40% (p < 0.001). Total PSQI-K scores rose in the CON group (+ 14.64 ± 22.44%) but declined in the ITSS group (- 38.90 ± 21.99%), showing a significant difference (p < 0.001). These findings suggest that ITSS enhances airflow by humidifying the nasal environment, thereby facilitating respiratory function and stabilizing ANS activity and brain function. This process ultimately contributes to improved overall sleep quality in young adults experiencing nasal congestion and irregular sleep patterns. The study was retrospectively registered on April 3, 2025, in the Clinical Research Information Service ( https://cris.nih.go.kr/cris/search/listDetail.do/ ) under registration number KCT0010381.

papers.title: Associations between dietary and lifestyle patterns and metabolic risk factors in the young adult population of Rwanda.
papers.abstract: Diet and lifestyle are key modifiable risk factors for the components of metabolic syndrome (MetS). In low- and middle-income countries undergoing nutrition transition, the relative importance of dietary patterns versus broader lifestyle, socio-demographic, and economic determinants of metabolic risk remains unclear, particularly among young adults. This study aimed to examine these associations in Rwanda. Between January and April 2023, a community-based cross-sectional survey was conducted among Rwandan adults aged 18-35 years (N = 699). Dietary intake was assessed with a validated food frequency questionnaire, and dietary patterns were derived using exploratory factor analysis. Lifestyle behaviour patterns were identified using latent class analysis based on seven risk behaviours. Metabolic risk factors were assessed following WHO STEP-wise approach. A Mixed-effect logistic regression, with province included as a random effect, examined associations between dietary/lifestyle patterns and MetS components, adjusting for socio-demographic and economic factors. Three dietary patterns were identified (Modern, Low-variety, and Traditional). Latent class analysis yielded two lifestyle classes: a lower-risk unhealthy lifestyle class (25.75%) and a higher-risk unhealthy lifestyle class (74.25%) characterized by greater probability of smoking, heavy episodic drinking, sedentary behaviour, inadequate sleep, and high salt intake. Individual metabolic risk factors were common (e.g., reduced high-density lipoprotein-cholesterol HDL-C: 25.9%; abdominal obesity: 20.3%), though MetS prevalence was low (5.4%). In multivariable-adjusted analyses, dietary patterns showed no independent associations with any MetS component. In contrast, the high-risk lifestyle pattern was positively associated with elevated fasting blood glucose (Odd Ratio, OR = 2.05, 95% Confidence Interval, CI: 1.14, 3.70) and inversely associated with abdominal obesity (OR = 0.36, 95% CI: 0.20, 0.67). Socio-demographic and economic factors, particularly sex, age, occupation, and urban/rural residence, showed strong and consistent associations with MetS components. Among young adults in Rwanda, lifestyle and socio-demographic and economic factors showed more consistent associations with metabolic risk indicators, whereas dietary patterns did not show independent associations. Future longitudinal investigations incorporating additional lifestyle factors and objective dietary assessment methods to overcome the inherent limitations of self-reported intake are warranted. In parallel, public health policy should prioritise targeted, community-based lifestyle interventions and socioeconomic disparity-reduction strategies to reduce metabolic risk among young adults. The study was registered as a clinical trial on November 27, 2019, at clinicaltrials.gov (reference number NCT04204538).

papers.title: Volunteer engagement in rural age-friendly care: a scoping review.
papers.abstract: Integrated, age-friendly care models are important in preventing functional decline and improving quality of life for older people. However, these models require an adequate, sufficiently trained workforce, which is challenging in rural areas. This study explores how volunteers contribute to age-friendly care in rural contexts, drawing on the Indigo 4Ms Framework (what matters, medication, mobility and mental wellbeing). A scoping review was undertaken following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Four databases (PsycINFO, Sociological Abstracts, Web of Science, and Scopus) were searched for rural-specific, English language studies published between 2013 and December 2025. Of 3,953 studies screened, 23 met criteria relating to rural volunteer-supported interventions that supported core elements of rural age-friendly care- what matters, medication, mobility and mental wellbeing. Volunteer involvement spanned all four core elements. All studies reported volunteer contributions to mental wellbeing through cognitive, social, sensory, hydration, nutrition, sleep, continence, and carer support activities. Almost two thirds examined volunteer support for what matters, and volunteer involvement in enhancing mobility, with one third examining volunteer roles in medication access, management, and safe use. There is evidence that volunteers can support all four elements of rural age-friendly care. Further research is needed to identify scope of practice for volunteers within rural age-friendly health care models, and to identify how volunteers can be best engaged in these models. Volunteer roles must be defined as supplementary, rather than as a substitute workforce.

papers.title: Parental knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding healthy sleep hygiene among children in Palestine.
papers.abstract: Children's sleep hygiene is a modifiable determinant of physical, emotional, behavioral, and academic well-being, yet parental knowledge and home practices remain underexplored in Palestine. This study assessed parental knowledge, practices, attitudes, and child sleep-related characteristics in a Palestinian sample. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted in Palestine between 7 March and 20 April 2026 using a Google Forms questionnaire. The survey covered child and family characteristics, sleep patterns, parental knowledge (15 items), sleep hygiene practices (15 items), sleep-related attitudes (6 items), sleep environment, and information sources. Of 461 responses received, 459 consenting participants were included in the analysis. Total scores were computed for knowledge (0-15), practices (15-75). Attitudes were summarized using frequency distributions for individual items. Implausible parent-age entries (< 18 years) and implausible computed sleep durations (< 4 or > 16 h) were treated as missing for analyses involving those variables. Descriptive statistics, reliability testing, non-parametric bivariate analyses, and multiple linear regression were performed. A total of 459 parents were analyzed; 96.7% were mothers, making our sample mainly maternal, and the mean child age was 7.30 ± 3.96 years. The mean school-night sleep duration was 9.27 ± 1.39 h, and 60.9% of children with valid school-night data met the 9-11-hour recommendation. Shared-room sleeping with siblings was common (57.5%), and 47.7% of families reported recent stressful circumstances affecting the child's sleep. The mean knowledge, practices scores were 12.14 ± 2.05 and 54.88 ± 12.51 respectively. In multivariable analyses, higher parental education and prior receipt of sleep information independently predicted higher knowledge scores, whereas low income predicted lower knowledge scores. Better practice scores were independently associated with village/camp residence and previous sleep information, and inversely associated with parental age, low income, and stressful family circumstances. Palestinian parents in this sample demonstrated generally good sleep-related knowledge but more modest implementation of healthy sleep hygiene practices. Economic strain, stressful family circumstances, and weaker access to sleep information were associated with poorer outcomes. Sleep education for parents, particularly for lower-income families and families living under recent stress, may improve the translation of knowledge into consistent bedtime practices.

papers.title: Molecular and electrophysiological properties underlying calcium signaling in muscle cells of ctenophores.
papers.abstract: Recent phylogenetic evidence placing ctenophores as a sister lineage to the rest of the animals has challenged existing views as to the origins of muscles, neurons, and nervous systems. Most of the electrophysiological and morphological data available for ctenophores predate the genomic age. An integrated cellular, genomic, and transcriptomic approach has yet to be employed in ctenophores; accordingly, little is known about how ctenophore cells detect, process, and coordinate internal and external signals. Here we show that excitable cells of the ctenophore Mnemiopsis neuromuscular system express a basic set of voltage-gated channels capable of generating and transmitting action potentials. Activation of those cells and generation of action potentials are accompanied by recurrent transient elevations in cytoplasmic Ca2+, allowing calcium imaging and evaluation of the activity of populations of sensory cells, neurons, and muscles. Despite the complex evolutionary histories of many of the channels, receptors, and specification factors involved in the operation and specification of these cell types, ctenophore excitable cells share core physiological and transcriptomic properties with those of cnidarians and bilaterians. Together, these data support an evolutionary scenario in which the muscle and neural cells of ctenophores, cnidarians, and bilaterians descended from an excitable cell present in the last common ancestor of animals.

papers.title: A novel homozygous missense variant in the GAMT gene causing cerebral creatine deficiency syndrome 2 in an Iranian patient: molecular dynamics insights and literature review.
papers.abstract: Cerebral creatine deficiency syndrome 2 (CCDS2; OMIM #612,736) is a rare autosomal recessive neurometabolic disorder caused by variants in the GAMT gene, leading to deficient creatine synthesis in the brain. Here, we report a 17-year-old Iranian Fars female patient from a consanguineous marriage presenting with severe intellectual disability, inability to walk, muscle atrophy, and epileptiform EEG activity. Whole-exome sequencing identified a previously unreported homozygous missense variant in GAMT (NM_000156.6: c.326A > G, p.Lys109Arg), classified as likely pathogenic according to ACMG guidelines. The affected lysine residue at position 109 is highly conserved across species. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations over 100 ns revealed that the p.Lys109Arg substitution induces a more compact global conformation (lower RMSD and Rg) but drastically alters the dynamic coupling network. Compared to wild-type, the mutant exhibited a substantially higher standard deviation in the cross-correlation matrix (0.323 vs. 0.236) and a markedly increased number of both strongly positive (4,006 vs. 1,574) and strongly negative (3,326 vs. 576) correlated residue pairs, indicating the emergence of extensive long-range allosteric perturbations that may disrupt functional dynamics and stability. Our report highlights the value of MD simulations as a tool to evaluate the structural consequences of genetic variants.

papers.title: The relationship between high-risk obstructive sleep apnea as identified by STOP-BANG questionnaire and diabetic retinopathy: a case-control observational study at a tertiary center in Jordan.
papers.abstract: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) remains a leading cause of vision loss worldwide. While metabolic control of blood glucose is the standard of care, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) has emerged as a potential systemic factor influencing retinal disease. This study investigated the association between OSA risk, as assessed by the STOP-BANG questionnaire, and the presence of DR in a Jordanian cohort. A case-control observational study was conducted at a tertiary center in Jordan, including 300 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus. Participants were divided into a disease group (moderate non-proliferative DR or worse and/or diabetic macular edema) and a control group (no DR). OSA risk was assessed using the STOP-BANG questionnaire. Clinical data were retrieved from electronic medical records. Multivariate logistic regression models were constructed with sequential adjustment for demographic, metabolic, and vascular factors. High-risk OSA category (as identified by the STOP-BANG questionnaire) was more frequent in the DR group compared with controls (odds ratio [OR]: 2.17; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.12-4.24; p = 0.023). This association remained significant after adjustment for age, sex, HbA1c, and duration of diabetes (adjusted OR: 2.12; 95% CI: 1.08-4.16; p = 0.029), and after further adjustment for hypertension and body mass index also (adjusted OR: 2.87; 95% CI: 1.10-7.50; p = 0.032). High-risk OSA category (as identified by the STOP-BANG questionnaire) was associated with DR in unadjusted and partially adjusted analyses. These findings suggest that the relationship between OSA high-risk category and DR is present in our cohort. However, further studies using objective OSA diagnostic methods are warranted.

papers.title: Effects of opioid-free intraoperative anesthesia versus opioid-based anesthesia on postoperative immune function in elderly patients undergoing total knee arthroplasty: a single-center, prospective, randomized controlled trial.
papers.abstract: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) in elderly patients may involve postoperative immune suppression. This study compares intraoperative opioid-free anesthesia (OFA) and opioid-based anesthesia (OBA) effects on postoperative proportion of immune cells. The core pharmacological difference between groups lies in the intraoperative anesthetic regimen: the OBA group received sufentanil for induction and continuous remifentanil infusion for maintenance, while the OFA group replaced all intraoperative opioids with esketamine. Both groups received opioid-containing patient-controlled intravenous analgesia and rescue analgesia after surgery, and the opioid-free anesthesia protocol was only applied during the intraoperative phase. A single-center, prospective, randomized controlled trial of 60 patients (60-80 years) undergoing unilateral TKA. The opioid-free strategy was exclusively implemented during the intraoperative period, and both groups received identical opioid-inclusive postoperative analgesia. Patients were randomized into OFA (n = 30) and OBA (n = 30) groups. change in natural killer (NK) cell proportion. T-cell subsets (CD3⁺, CD4⁺, CD8⁺), B cells, dynamic/static visual analogue scale (VAS) scores, patient-controlled intravenous analgesia (PCIA) demands, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), hemodynamics, and adverse events. We conducted an intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis in 60 patients (30 in each group). Baseline demographics and preoperative immune indices showed no significant differences between the groups. Compared with the levels one day before the operation, the postoperative reduction in NK cell proportion was significantly smaller in the OFA group than in the OBA group (Δ = -5.51% ± 4.89% vs. Δ = -10.12% ± 5.39%; P < 0.001). The OFA group demonstrated superior early postoperative analgesia, with lower dynamic and static VAS scores at 4-48 h (P < 0.05), reduced PCIA demands at 24 h (5.8 ± 0.9 vs. 7.2 ± 1.1) and 48 h (6.1 ± 1.0 vs. 8.5 ± 1.3; P < 0.05), and better PSQI (7.50 ± 3.34 vs. 10.86 ± 4.01; P < 0.001). The OFA group had significantly lower intraoperative vasoactive agent consumption (atropine, norepinephrine, ephedrine) and 72-hour postoperative opioid consumption (all P < 0.05), and exhibited superior postoperative functional exercise capacity (active knee flexion angle and maximum walking distance) at 48 and 72 h postoperatively (all P < 0.05). No significant differences were observed between the groups in CD8⁺ T cell, B cell proportions, extubation time, length of hospital stay, rescue analgesia rate or postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) incidence (all P > 0.05). In elderly patients undergoing unilateral total knee arthroplasty, intraoperative esketamine-based opioid-free anesthesia was associated with a smaller decline in NK-cell proportion, superior early analgesia, and improved short-term sleep quality compared with opioid-based anesthesia. These findings are limited to the comparison of intraoperative strategies and cannot be extrapolated to full perioperative opioid-free management. Chinese clinical trial registry, ID: ChiCTR2300069836; Date: 27/03/2023.

papers.title: Circadian syndrome and headache accompanied by stomach pain among middle-aged and older Chinese adults: associations and the mediating role of frailty.
papers.abstract: Circadian syndrome (CircS) integrates metabolic abnormalities, short sleep duration, and depressive symptoms, and may reflect multidimensional circadian-related health dysregulation. Migraine is a disabling neurological disorder that is frequently accompanied by gastrointestinal symptoms, but evidence on the association between CircS and migraine-related symptom phenotypes in middle-aged and older adults remains limited. This study examined the associations between CircS and headache accompanied by stomach pain, a self-reported symptom co-occurrence phenotype, and explored the mediating role of frailty. Data were obtained from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. A total of 9,342 participants were included in the cross-sectional analysis, and 5,895 participants without headache accompanied by stomach pain at baseline were included in the longitudinal analysis. CircS was defined as the presence of at least four of seven components. Logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models were used to examine the associations of CircS with prevalent and incident headache accompanied by stomach pain, respectively. Sensitivity analyses included complete-case analyses, a 2-year lag analysis, age-restricted analysis, propensity score matching, and E-value analysis. Time-dependent receiver operating characteristic curves and bootstrap mediation analysis were also performed. CircS was associated with higher odds of prevalent headache accompanied by stomach pain after full adjustment (OR = 1.38, 95% CI: 1.14-1.67, p < 0.001). During follow-up, 969 participants developed incident headache accompanied by stomach pain. CircS was associated with an increased risk of incident headache accompanied by stomach pain (HR = 1.33, 95% CI: 1.16-1.51), and the risk increased with greater CircS component burden. Sensitivity analyses generally supported the main findings. CircS showed numerically higher discriminative ability than metabolic syndrome and individual CircS components. Frailty explained 19.72% of the association between CircS and incident headache accompanied by stomach pain (p < 0.001). Among middle-aged and older Chinese adults, CircS was associated with prevalent and incident headache accompanied by stomach pain, and frailty partially explained this association. As the outcome was based on self-reported symptom co-occurrence, it should not be equated with clinically diagnosed migraine.

papers.title: Environmental enrichment during adolescence ameliorates anxiety-related corticosterone, enhances memory, and is associated with changes in regional dopamine levels in the Wistar Kyoto rat, a putative model of endogenous depression.
papers.abstract: Adolescence is a critical period in neurodevelopment marked by heightened plasticity, cognitive enhancement, and susceptibility to stress-induced impairments. The Wistar-Kyoto rat displays anxiety- and depressive-like behaviours, dysregulated stress responses and cognitive deficits, making it ideal for studying the effect of environmental interventions. Here, effects of environmental enrichment (EE) were assessed on anxiety, cognition, peripheral markers and monoaminergic levels. Male and female WKY were exposed to EE from postnatal day 22 onwards and assessed as mid-, late adolescents or young adults using novel object recognition, elevated plus maze (EPM), and radial arm maze paradigms. Serum and brain dopamine (DA), serotonin (5-HT), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and corticosterone (CORT) were quantified by ELISA and LC-MS/MS. Results demonstrated that EE enhanced recognition memory (p < 0.0001) in adolescents, and spatial memory (p < 0.0001) in young adults. Peripherally, CORT decreased. During mid-adolescence, EE increased prefrontal DA (p = 0.006) in females, and caudate putamen and Nucleus accumbens DA in both sexes. During late adolescence, EE increased caudate putamen DA (p = 0.006) in females and Nucleus accumbens DA in males (p = 0.03). Correlational analyses indicated that recognition memory was associated with prefrontal and striatal DA levels, while anxiety correlated with CORT levels and prefrontal 5-HT levels, indicating that EE may enhance cognition and reduce anxiety with associated changes in DA levels. Given that the WKY depicts some face, construct and predictive validities of anxiety and depression, EE-based strategies may offer therapeutic potential for stress-related cognitive and emotional disorders in adolescents.

papers.title: Independent and joint associations of social determinants of health and circadian syndrome with serum testosterone in adult males.
papers.abstract: To examine the association of a multidomain social determinants of health (SDoH) score with serum testosterone and to determine whether circadian syndrome (CircS) modifies this association in adult men. This cross-sectional study included 5,089 men from NHANES 2011-2016. Survey-weighted linear regression evaluated associations of an eight-component cumulative SDoH score and individual components with testosterone. Interaction terms assessed effect modification by CircS. Sensitivity analyses included a six-component score excluding marital and housing status. In the fully adjusted model, each one-unit higher SDoH score was associated with 6.46 ng/dL higher testosterone (95% CI 3.81-9.10; P < 0.001), with a positive association across categories. Five component-specific associations were significant, not being married or living with a partner having the largest point estimate and housing tenure being another notable association. Excluding marital and housing status attenuated the association, but the six-component score remained significant (β = 4.97, 95% CI 1.72-8.23; P = 0.003). CircS modified the association (P for interaction = 0.010): it was positive in men without CircS (β = 7.94, 95% CI 5.12-10.76; P < 0.001) but not significant in men with CircS (β = -1.12, 95% CI - 7.59-5.35; P = 0.735). Multiple imputation and other sensitivity analyses supported the primary finding. Higher SDoH scores were associated with higher testosterone, with heterogeneous component-specific associations and attenuation in the presence of CircS. The cross-sectional design precludes causal inference.

papers.title: The relationship between emotion dysregulation and subjective and objective sleep difficulties from late pregnancy to early postpartum.
papers.abstract: The perinatal period is marked by rapid changes in one's life that can increase the risk of sleep difficulties and emotion dysregulation (ED). While the relationship between ED and sleep is well-documented, it remains understudied in the perinatal period despite the resulting adverse maternal-infant outcomes. This study aimed to address gaps in our understanding by (1) examining the relationship between ED and sleep longitudinally from late pregnancy to early postpartum and by (2) using both subjective and objective measures of sleep. Fifty-eight participants were assessed during their third trimester of pregnancy and at 1-3 and 6-12 weeks postpartum. ED was assessed using the Difficulties In Emotion Regulation Scale at visit 1. Participants wore actigraphs for 2-week periods to obtain objective sleep data at each timepoint, including total sleep time, sleep efficiency (SE), wake after sleep onset (WASO), sleep onset latency, and awakenings. Subjective sleep quality was examined using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Subjective sleep quality differed significantly between participants who had high ED compared to those with low ED at all visits. Further, the high ED group experienced worse sleep quality. Significant differences in this direction were also found for SE and WASO during the third trimester of pregnancy. This study provides support for the differential influence of ED on subjective and objective sleep across the third trimester of pregnancy to 1-3 and 6-12 weeks postpartum. With its use of a longitudinal design and subjective and objective sleep measures, this study provides novel insights into the ED-sleep relationship perinatally. The relationship between emotion dysregulation (ED) and sleep is understudied in the perinatal period, despite the resulting adverse maternal-infant outcomes. To address this gap, this study examined the relationship between ED and sleep longitudinally from late pregnancy to early postpartum using both subjective and objective sleep measures. This study provides support for the differential influence of ED on subjective and objective sleep across the third trimester of pregnancy to 1-3 and 6-12 weeks postpartum. The use of a longitudinal design and inclusion of both objective and subjective sleep measures provides novel insights into the ED - sleep relationship perinatally.

papers.title: Evening amber-lensed glasses in combination with a prescribed wake time advance circadian timing in adolescents with delayed sleep-wake phase disorder.
papers.abstract: We tested whether wearing amber glasses during evening hours and a stable wake time advances circadian and sleep timing of adolescent patients with delayed sleep-wake phase disorder (DSWPD). Adolescents (14.3-18.1 years; n = 36 randomized) with DSWPD completed a 3-week study. Dim light melatonin onset (DLMO) was measured after 1 week of habitual sleep/wake. During the next 2 weeks, participants were randomized to one of two groups: the treatment group wore amber-lensed glasses, and a control group wore clear-lensed glasses nightly, starting 7 h before midpoint of baseline sleep, and ending at self-selected bedtime or for 7 h, whichever was shorter. Treatment group participants were additionally instructed to wake at their average baseline school-day wake time (± 15 min). Final DLMO was measured at the end. The treatment group advanced 40 ± 84 min and the control group delayed - 29 ± 50 min [t(26) = - 2.63, p = .01]. Despite circadian phase changes, weeknight sleep onset and duration remained stable with the amber glasses + stable wake intervention. Weekday wake-up time did not differ between groups; however, the Treatment group woke earlier on weekends during the glasses weeks compared to the Control group [t(25) = 4.13, p < .001], resulting in more stable sleep times across the week. Amber glasses in the evening with fixed wake times shifted circadian phase earlier among adolescents with DSWPD. Although sleep onset did not advance, sleep timing was more consistent across the week. This strategy represents a readily implemented cost-effective intervention to advance the circadian clock and reduce social jet lag in a difficult-to-treat young patient group. Additional directives may be needed to effect other sleep-related outcomes. Current knowledge/study rationale Adolescent patients with DSWPD are at high risk for deleterious sleep-related outcomes. Feasible and effective treatment interventions are sparse. Amber glasses timed strategically in the evening with a fixed wake time was associated with circadian phase advances and reduced sleep variability. This intervention is cost-effective and readily implemented. Since physiological changes did not translate into changes in additional sleep/wake behaviors, however, future treatment approaches need to be further refined and delineated.
